If multiple providers with the same highest order are present on the classpath, the selected provider depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. Since the previous fail-fast behavior for multiple providers was removed, a misconfigured classpath may silently select an unintended provider. A deterministic tie-breaker or an error on equal highest order would be safer."

AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns the provider of the default KeyStore type, which may be SUN, SunJSSE, or another unrelated provider. Callers that rely on the returned provider or its name may attempt to use algorithms that are not provided or may get unexpected behavior. If no BouncyCastle provider is available, returning null or a clearly documented fallback would be less misleading."

If the supplied signature is shorter than expected, System.arraycopy throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; if it is longer, trailing bytes are silently ignored. A self-consistent but non-standard DER encoding could pass this test while failing interoperability. findings.title: New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public extension point. Adding int order() without a default method breaks source and binary compatibility for external implementations. At runtime CryptoIntegration.detectProvider sorts providers with Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order), so an older implementation that does not have this method will cause AbstractMethodError. A default method should be added to preserve compatibility.

findings.title: Provider selection is nondeterministic when order values tie
findings.body: detectProvider sorts providers only by order() in descending order. DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200. If multiple providers with the same highest order are present on the classpath, the selected provider depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. Since the previous fail-fast behavior for multiple providers was removed, a misconfigured classpath may silently select an unintended provider. A deterministic tie-breaker or an error on equal highest order would be safer.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns an unrelated JCE provider
findings.body: CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider is documented as returning the BouncyCastle, or FIPS BouncyCastle, provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns the provider of the default KeyStore type, which may be SUN, SunJSSE, or another unrelated provider. Callers that rely on the returned provider or its name may attempt to use algorithms that are not provided or may get unexpected behavior. If no BouncyCastle provider is available, returning null or a clearly documented fallback would be less misleading.

findings.title: ECDSA raw-to-DER conversion does not validate signature length
findings.body: concatenatedRSToASN1DER computes len = signLength / 2 and copies len bytes from offset 0 and len bytes from offset len without checking that signature.length == signLength, that signLength is positive, or that it is even. If the supplied signature is shorter than expected, System.arraycopy throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; if it is longer, trailing bytes are silently ignored. Malformed input should be rejected with IOException or IllegalArgumentException.

findings.title: integerToBytes silently truncates oversized or malformed integers
findings.body: In asn1derToConcatenatedRS, integerToBytes copies the last qLength bytes whenever BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than qLength. This is only correct when the extra byte is a leading zero sign byte for a positive integer. The method does not check that the BigInteger is positive, that the value fits in qLength, or that discarded bytes are zero. A malformed or oversized DER integer can therefore be silently converted into an incorrect fixed-length R/S coordinate instead of being rejected.

findings.title: Indefinite or negative ASN.1 lengths can cause NegativeArraySizeException
findings.body: ASN1Decoder.readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, but readInteger passes that value directly to read(int), which allocates new byte[length]. Malformed DER input with an indefinite length therefore causes NegativeArraySizeException instead of a controlled IOException. readSequence also treats a -1 length as an empty sequence rather than rejecting it. The decoder should explicitly reject indefinite and negative lengths.

findings.title: readSequence does not enforce the declared SEQUENCE length
findings.body: readSequence subtracts each parsed child TLV length from the declared sequence length and stops when the remaining length is no longer positive. If a child TLV is longer than the remaining declared length, the remaining length becomes negative and parsing stops without error. This accepts malformed DER instead of rejecting it. The parser should throw when the remaining length becomes negative or when the declared content is not consumed exactly.

findings.title: ECDSA conversion test only checks self-roundtrip, not standard DER validity
findings.body: The test converts a Java-produced DER signature to concatenated R/S and back, then asserts that the two concatenated arrays are equal. It does not verify that the regenerated DER signature is accepted by java.security.Signature.verify, and it uses a default EC key pair rather than curve-specific keys for ES384/ES512. A self-consistent but non-standard DER encoding could pass this test while failing interoperability. The test should verify the regenerated DER with the public key and/or use known test vectors for each curve.
